---
title: "Quiz: reconstruction and h-extrema"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Reconstruction $R_A(M)$: dilate the marker $M$ one step, clip it to the mask $A$, repeat until nothing changes. Grey levels: the same with max/min; $\mathrm{HMAX}_h(I) = R_I(I - h)$, $\mathrm{HMIN}_h(I) = R^{\varepsilon}_I(I + h)$.

---

**Q1.** A mask contains 30 cells and many specks. You put one seed pixel in each of 5 cells and reconstruct. What is the result?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How far can the marker grow, and where must it stop?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Exactly the 5 seeded cells, complete and unchanged; the other 25 cells and all specks are gone. The marker grows through every pixel connected to a seed inside the mask, and cannot leave the mask.
:::

---

**Q2.** Why does an opening by reconstruction keep thin bridges and protrusions that an ordinary opening removes?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What role does the erosion play in each case?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
In the ordinary opening, the erosion result is dilated back by the SE: only what the SE reaches comes back, so thin parts stay lost. In the opening by reconstruction, the erosion is only a marker: it says which components contain a part the SE fits into. The reconstruction then floods each such component completely, bridges and protrusions included.
:::

---

**Q3.** How do you remove all objects that touch the image border with a reconstruction? And how do you fill holes?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Choose the marker and the mask.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Clear border: marker = object pixels on the frame (the outermost rows and columns), mask = the objects; the reconstruction is the set of objects touching the border; subtract it from the mask. Fill holes: marker = background pixels on the frame, mask = the background; the reconstruction is the background reachable from outside; everything else (the holes) becomes object. Use 4-connected steps for the background, 8-connected for objects.
:::

---

**Q4.** In 1D, what is $R_I(M)$ for $I = 3\,5\,2\,6\,1$ and a seed only at the 6, i.e. $M = 0\,0\,0\,6\,0$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each step: max over the 3-window, then min with $I$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Step 1: $0\,0\,6\,6\,6 \to$ clipped: $0\,0\,2\,6\,1$. Step 2: $0\,2\,6\,6\,6 \to 0\,2\,2\,6\,1$. Step 3: $2\,2\,6\,6\,6 \to 2\,2\,2\,6\,1$. Step 4: no change. Result $2\,2\,2\,6\,1$: the seed's hill is kept, and to the left the flood can only pass at the level of the pass, 2.
:::

---

**Q5.** A noisy image of nuclei has thousands of regional maxima. How does the h-maxima transform reduce them, and what does $h$ mean in grey levels?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How deep must you go down from a maximum to reach a higher one?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\mathrm{HMAX}_h$ lowers every peak by $h$ and flattens every peak whose **dynamic** (the descent needed to reach a higher point) is at most $h$. Noise bumps have dynamics of a few noise standard deviations; a nucleus rises far above the background. With $h$ above the noise bumps but below the nucleus contrast, one regional maximum per nucleus remains. (Touching nuclei separated by a shallow neck may still merge.)
:::

---

**Q6.** What does $\mathrm{HMIN}_h$ do to a basin of depth 5 and to one of depth 2, for $h = 3$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Water up to $h$ above the bottom, but never above the spill level.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The basin of depth 5 is filled by 3: its bottom rises by 3, it remains a regional minimum (2 deep). The basin of depth 2 is filled to its spill level and merges with its neighbour: it is no longer a minimum. This is how the watershed day removes noise basins before flooding.
:::

---

**Q7.** Why is reconstruction by iterated geodesic dilation slow on a large image, and what does the fast algorithm do differently?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many pixels change in one iteration?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each iteration visits every pixel, but only the pixels on the moving front change; a flood across a 200-pixel object needs about 200 iterations, so the cost is (number of pixels) × (number of iterations). The fast algorithm keeps a first-in-first-out queue of front pixels and only processes those; each pixel is handled a small number of times, so the cost is linear in the number of pixels.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Does $R_A(M)$ depend on the SE used in each geodesic step? Compare the $3 \times 3$ square with the $5 \times 5$ square (clipping after each step in both cases).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Characterise the result as the components of $A$ that meet $M$. Can a step with the $5 \times 5$ square cross a one-pixel gap?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
With the $3 \times 3$ square the result is the union of the 8-connected components of $A$ that meet $M$: the marker spreads to every pixel connected to it inside $A$, and never leaves a component. With the $5 \times 5$ square the marker can jump over a one-pixel gap of background, so it can enter a different component of $A$ that is 2 pixels away: the result can be larger. So it does depend on the SE: the SE defines the connectivity. Larger steps give the same result only if the components of $A$ are at least as far apart as the SE reaches.
:::
